questions.question: Which group of words is a dependent clause?
options: Please approve the request
Unless the supervisor approves the request
Approve the request today
The supervisor approved the request
The request was approved
questions.explanation: A dependent clause has a subject and verb but begins with a subordinating word (unless), so it cannot stand alone. The other choices are independent clauses.

questions.question: In "She resigned because the salary was low," the clause "because the salary was low" is a(n):
options: adjective clause
independent clause
adverb clause
prepositional phrase
noun clause
questions.explanation: The clause tells why she resigned, so it modifies the verb and is an adverb (dependent) clause.

questions.question: Which sentence contains only one independent clause?
options: The bell rang; the students left.
The bell rang, and the students left.
The bell rang, but the students stayed.
When the bell rang, the students left the room.
The bell rang, so the students left.
questions.explanation: "When the bell rang" is dependent, leaving only one independent clause. The others join two independent clauses.

questions.question: Which word begins an adjective (relative) clause?
options: unless
while
because
although
who
questions.explanation: Relative pronouns such as who, which, and that start adjective clauses; the others are subordinating conjunctions that start adverb clauses.

questions.question: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: Although the road was flooded, the drivers continued their trip.
The road was flooded, but the drivers continued.
The road was flooded, and the drivers stopped.
The road was flooded; the drivers stopped.
The drivers continued and finished the trip.
questions.explanation: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. Only the first has a dependent clause (Although...).

questions.question: In "I know that she will pass the exam," the clause "that she will pass the exam" functions as a:
options: independent clause
noun clause serving as the direct object of "know"
appositive phrase
adjective clause modifying "I"
adverb clause modifying "pass"
questions.explanation: The clause answers "know what?", so it acts as a noun (direct object); it is a dependent noun clause.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a restrictive relative clause correctly?
options: The employee who, won the award works in Cebu.
The employee whom won the award works in Cebu.
The employee who won the award works in Cebu.
The employee who won, the award works in Cebu.
The employee, who won the award works in Cebu.
questions.explanation: A restrictive clause identifies which employee and takes no commas; "whom" is wrong because the clause needs a subject form (who).

questions.question: Which sentence is a compound sentence?
options: Stamping the forms, the clerk smiled.
The clerk who stamped the forms left early.
The clerk stamped and signed the forms.
The clerk stamped the forms, and the officer signed them.
After the clerk stamped the forms, she left.
questions.explanation: A compound sentence joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction (and). The others have a dependent clause or a compound predicate.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates a nonrestrictive clause?
options: My supervisor, who has served for twenty years will retire in June.
My supervisor who, has served for twenty years will retire in June.
My supervisor who has served for twenty years, will retire in June.
My supervisor; who has served for twenty years, will retire in June.
My supervisor, who has served for twenty years, will retire in June.
questions.explanation: A nonrestrictive clause adds extra information and must be set off by a pair of commas at both ends.

questions.question: Which choice correctly joins the two independent clauses? "The deadline was extended ___ some applicants still failed to submit."
options: ; however,
however,
, which
, because
, however,
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by a conjunctive adverb (however) need a semicolon before it; a comma alone causes a comma splice.

questions.question: Which sentence contains an error in subject-verb agreement within a dependent clause?
options: The files, which are old, belong to the director.
The file that is on the desk belongs to the director.
The files that is on the desk belong to the director.
The files on the desk belong to the director.
The files that are on the desk belong to the director.
questions.explanation: "That" refers to the plural "files," so the relative clause needs "are", not "is".

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses "whom" in a dependent clause?
options: The applicant whom she is was hired.
The applicant whom is qualified was hired.
The applicant whom was interviewed was hired.
The applicant whom the panel interviewed was hired.
The applicant whom interviewed the panel was hired.
questions.explanation: "Whom" is the object of "interviewed" in its clause (the panel interviewed whom). In the others, the pronoun would need to be the subject (who).

questions.question: Which sentence has a misplaced relative clause?
options: The report that was full of errors was given to the clerk.
The clerk received a report that was full of errors.
The manager gave the clerk a report that was full of errors.
The manager gave the clerk the report, which was full of errors.
The manager gave a report to the clerk that was full of errors.
questions.explanation: "That was full of errors" should sit beside "report," not "clerk." A relative clause must follow the word it modifies.

questions.question: In "Whoever submits the form first will receive the slot," the clause "Whoever submits the form first" is a:
options: noun clause serving as the subject
adverb clause of time
independent clause
adjective clause modifying "form"
noun clause serving as the object
questions.explanation: "Whoever submits the form first" is the doer of "will receive," so it is a dependent noun clause acting as subject.

questions.question: Choose the parallel completion: "The new employee is punctual, honest, and ___."
options: works hard
hardworking
has been working hard
a hard worker
she works hard
questions.explanation: A series must use the same grammatical form; punctual, honest, and hardworking are all adjectives.

questions.question: Which sentence keeps its series of -ing words parallel?
options: She enjoys cooking, jogging, and to paint.
She enjoys cook, jog, and painting.
She enjoys cooking, jogging, and painting.
She enjoys to cook, jogging, and painting.
She enjoys cooking, to jog, and painting.
questions.explanation: All three items are gerunds (-ing forms), so the series is parallel.

questions.question: Choose the correct completion: "You may pay in cash, by check, or ___."
options: if you use a credit card
with a credit card being used
credit card
by credit card
using a credit card, too
questions.explanation: The phrases "in cash," "by check," and "by credit card" are all prepositional phrases, keeping the series parallel.

questions.question: Which sentence mixes nouns with a phrase in a series, making it faulty in parallelism?
options: The job requires accuracy, speed, and care.
The job requires patience, accuracy, and punctuality.
The job requires patience and accuracy.
The job requires being patient, accurate, and punctual.
The job requires patience, accuracy, and being on time.
questions.explanation: "Patience" and "accuracy" are nouns, but "being on time" is a phrase. Use the noun "punctuality" to match.

questions.question: Choose the correct completion: "The clerk not only typed the letter but also ___."
options: mailed it
the mailing of it
was mailing it
he mailed it
it was mailed
questions.explanation: After "not only ... but also" both parts must match; "typed the letter" and "mailed it" are both past-tense verb phrases.

questions.question: Which sentence keeps its list of commands parallel?
options: Employees should arrive on time, wearing their IDs, and follow the rules.
Employees should arrive on time, wear their IDs, and follow the rules.
Employees should arrival on time, wear their IDs, and follow the rules.
Employees should arrive on time, to wear their IDs, and following the rules.
Employees should arrive on time, their IDs wear, and follow the rules.
questions.explanation: Arrive, wear, and follow are all base-form verbs with the same structure.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses correlative conjunctions?
options: She is neither rude nor she is lazy.
She is neither rude or lazy.
She is neither rude nor lazy.
She is neither rude, or lazy.
She is neither rude nor working lazily.
questions.explanation: "Neither" must pair with "nor," and the two items (rude, lazy) must be the same part of speech.

questions.question: Choose the parallel completion: "Mr. Cruz is respected for his honesty, his skill, and ___."
options: that he gives
being generous
generously
his generosity
he is generous
questions.explanation: The series uses "his + noun" (his honesty, his skill, his generosity).

questions.question: Which sentence is NOT parallel in its series of clauses and nouns?
options: The report was clearly written and accurate.
The report was clear, well organized, and accurate.
The report was clear, organized, and accurate.
The report was clear and accurate.
The report was clear, well organized, and it was accurate.
questions.explanation: Two adjectives are followed by a full clause ("it was accurate"). All items should be adjectives.

questions.question: Choose the best revision: "The director wants to hire someone who is experienced and with a good attitude."
options: The director wants to hire someone who is experienced and has a good attitude.
The director wants to hire someone with experience and has a good attitude.
The director wants to hire someone who is experienced and a good attitude.
The director wants to hire someone experienced and having a good attitude too.
The director wants to hire someone who is experienced and with having a good attitude.
questions.explanation: "Who is experienced and has a good attitude" gives two matching predicates joined by "and," fixing the unbalanced adjective + phrase.

questions.question: Which sentence is parallel in a comparison?
options: It is better for prevention than to correct a problem.
It is better to prevent a problem than to correct one.
It is better preventing a problem than to correct one.
It is better to prevent a problem than correction of one.
It is better to prevent a problem than correcting one.
questions.explanation: Comparisons require matching forms: "to prevent" is balanced with "to correct."

questions.question: Which sentence is NOT parallel in its list of noun elements?
options: The speaker explained what the policy covers, who may apply, and when to file.
The speaker explained the coverage, eligibility, and deadlines.
The speaker explained what the policy covers, who may apply, and the deadlines.
The speaker explained what is covered, who qualifies, and when to file.
The speaker explained the policy, the applicants, and the deadlines.
questions.explanation: Two noun clauses are followed by a bare noun ("the deadlines"). It should be a clause such as "when the deadlines are."

questions.question: Choose the best revision: "The committee reviewed the proposal, rejected the budget, and a new plan was requested."
options: The committee reviewed the proposal, rejected the budget, and a new plan was requested by it.
The committee reviewed the proposal, the budget was rejected, and requested a new plan.
The committee reviewed the proposal, rejected the budget, and then a new plan.
The committee reviewed the proposal, rejected the budget, and requested a new plan.
The committee was reviewing the proposal, rejected the budget, and requests a new plan.
questions.explanation: The sentence shifts from active verbs to a passive clause. All three predicates should be active past-tense verbs with the same subject.

questions.question: Which sentence balances its either/or phrases in parallel form?
options: Whether you apply online or to appear in person, you must bring a valid ID.
Whether applying online or you go in person, you must bring a valid ID.
Whether online application or you appear in person, you must bring a valid ID.
Whether you apply online or by going in person, you must bring a valid ID.
Whether you apply online or in person, you must bring a valid ID.
questions.explanation: "Online" and "in person" are both adverbial expressions of manner and balance each other.

questions.question: Which sentence is NOT parallel in its list of criteria?
options: Applicants will be judged on how well they write, their speaking ability, and how they solve problems.
Applicants will be judged on writing, speaking, and problem solving.
Applicants will be judged on how well they write, how well they speak, and how well they solve problems.
Applicants will be judged on their writing, their speaking, and their problem solving.
Applicants will be judged on how they write, speak, and solve problems.
questions.explanation: A noun clause, a noun phrase, and another noun clause are mixed. Items must all be clauses or all be noun phrases.

questions.question: Which sentence has a misplaced prepositional phrase?
options: The clerk handed the blue folder to the applicant.
The clerk handed the form to the applicant with a blue folder.
The clerk handed the applicant the form.
The clerk handed the form to the applicant quickly.
The clerk with a blue folder handed the form to the applicant.
questions.explanation: "With a blue folder" is ambiguous; it is far from the noun it describes. Phrases should be placed next to the words they modify.

questions.question: In which sentence is the modifier correctly placed?
options: I bought a loaf of fresh this morning bread.
I a fresh bought loaf of bread this morning.
I bought a loaf of bread fresh this morning.
I bought a fresh loaf of bread this morning.
Fresh, I bought a loaf of bread this morning.
questions.explanation: The adjective "fresh" belongs directly before the noun phrase it modifies.

questions.question: Which sentence uses "only" so that it means no one else attended?
options: Ana attended only the seminar.
Ana attended the seminar only.
Ana only attended the seminar.
Ana attended the only seminar.
Only Ana attended the seminar.
questions.explanation: "Only" placed right before "Ana" limits the meaning to her alone. Moving it changes what it modifies.

questions.question: Choose the best revision: "Covered in dust, the clerk found the old files."
options: The clerk, covered in dust, finding the old files.
The clerk found the old files covered in dust.
The clerk found the old files, and covered in dust.
Covered in dust, the clerk found the old files.
Covered in dust, a clerk's old files were found.
questions.explanation: The files were covered in dust, so the phrase must be next to "files." Otherwise it misplaces the modifier on "clerk."

questions.question: Which sentence means that the auditor examined just the ledger and nothing else?
options: The auditor only examined the ledger.
The auditor examined the only ledger.
The auditor examined only the ledger.
Only the auditor examined the ledger.
The auditor examined the ledger, only.
questions.explanation: "Only" placed directly before "the ledger" limits the object examined; other placements change what is limited (the verb, the doer, or the ledger count).

questions.question: Which sentence has a squinting modifier?
options: Employees who complain are often ignored.
Employees who complain get ignored often.
Employees who complain are ignored.
Employees who complain often get ignored.
Employees who often complain get ignored.
questions.explanation: "Often" could modify either "complain" or "get ignored." A squinting modifier fits two words, making the meaning unclear.

questions.question: Choose the best revision: "To get a better score, extra hours must be spent reviewing."
options: To get a better score, extra hours reviewing must be spent.
To get a better score, reviewing is where extra hours go.
To get a better score, spending of extra hours is a must.
To get a better score, extra hours must be spent by reviewing.
To get a better score, you must spend extra hours reviewing.
questions.explanation: The infinitive phrase needs a doer as the subject (you). The original leaves the modifier dangling.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly attaches its introductory participial phrase?
options: Having completed the audit, the accountant submitted the findings.
Having completed the audit, the findings were submitted by the accountant.
Having completed the audit, submission of the findings was done.
Having completed the audit, it was the findings the accountant submitted.
Having completed the audit, the findings were submitted.
questions.explanation: "Having completed" must modify the one who did the completing (the accountant), who must be the subject of the main clause.

questions.question: Which sentence is clear about who was wearing a uniform?
options: The guard stopped the visitor, in a uniform.
The guard in a uniform stopped the visitor.
In a uniform, the visitor was stopped by the guard, clearly.
The guard stopped in a uniform the visitor.
The guard stopped the visitor and in a uniform.
questions.explanation: The prepositional phrase "in a uniform" sits directly after "guard," the noun it modifies, so there is no confusion.

questions.question: Which sentence has a misplaced modifier that changes who has the red marks?
options: The teacher returned the marked papers to the students.
The teacher returned the students' papers, which had red marks.
The teacher returned the papers to the students with red marks.
The teacher returned the papers with red marks to the students.
With red marks, the papers were returned to the students.
questions.explanation: "With red marks" is next to "students," suggesting the students had red marks; it should be next to "papers."

questions.question: Choose the best revision: "Driving through the province, the mountains were beautiful."
options: The mountains were beautiful, driving through the province.
Driving through the province, the mountains were beautiful to see.
Driving through the province, the beautiful mountains were seen.
Driving through the province, we found the mountains beautiful.
Driving through the province, the mountains' beauty was clear.
questions.explanation: The participial phrase needs a human subject (we); "the mountains" cannot drive. Adding "we" fixes the dangling modifier.

questions.question: Which sentence has a properly attached opening phrase?
options: Wanting to be fair, everyone's turn to speak was given.
Wanting to be fair, speaking turns were given out.
Wanting to be fair, a turn was given to everyone.
Wanting to be fair, everyone was given a turn by the rules.
Wanting to be fair, the director gave everyone a turn to speak.
questions.explanation: The subject "the director" is the one wanting to be fair, so the modifier is attached properly.

questions.question: Which sentence expresses that only the report, and nothing else, was reviewed by the editor?
options: The editor reviewed only the report.
The editor only reviewed the report.
The editor reviewed the report only yesterday.
The editor reviewed the only report.
Only the editor reviewed the report.
questions.explanation: "Only" directly before "the report" limits the object reviewed. Other placements limit the editor, the verb, or the time.

questions.question: Which is a sentence fragment?
options: The flight was delayed by the storm.
The storm delayed the flight.
Delayed by the storm, the flight arrived late.
The flight, delayed by the storm, arrived late.
Which was delayed by the storm.
questions.explanation: "Which was delayed by the storm" is a relative clause without a main clause. It cannot stand alone.

questions.question: Which choice corrects the fragment "After the training ended on Friday."?
options: After the training ended on Friday, the participants went home.
After the training ended on Friday, going home.
After the training ended on Friday, which was long.
After the training ended on Friday and the participants.
After the training, which ended on Friday.
questions.explanation: Attaching an independent clause to the dependent clause makes a complete sentence.

questions.question: Which sentence is the most concise and clear?
options: On the day of Monday, the committee is going to be meeting together.
The committee, it will meet on Monday.
The committee will meet on Monday.
There will be a meeting by the committee on Monday.
The committee will have a meeting that is on the day of Monday.
questions.explanation: Wordiness and redundancy are removed; the sentence says the same thing in fewer words.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly fixes the run-on "I submitted the form the clerk lost it"?
options: I submitted the form, the clerk, lost it.
I submitted the form, the clerk lost it.
I submitted the form but, the clerk lost it.
I submitted the form, but the clerk lost it.
I submitted the form the clerk, lost it.
questions.explanation: A comma plus a coordinating conjunction (but) properly joins two independent clauses.

questions.question: Which sentence has an ambiguous pronoun reference?
options: The director announced the new policy when meeting the secretary.
When the director met her, the secretary announced the new policy.
The director met the secretary and announced the new policy.
When the director met the secretary, the director announced the new policy.
When the director met the secretary, she announced the new policy.
questions.explanation: "She" could refer to either the director or the secretary, so the pronoun reference is unclear; the other choices name the doer.

questions.question: Which sentence handles neither/nor agreement correctly?
options: Neither the manager nor the clerks were present at the meeting.
Neither the manager nor the clerks are were present at the meeting.
Neither the manager or the clerks were present at the meeting.
Neither the manager nor the clerks being present at the meeting.
Neither the manager nor the clerks was present at the meeting.
questions.explanation: With "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject (clerks), which is plural, so "were" is correct.

questions.question: Which is the best way to combine: "The report was long. It was well written. It was ignored."?
options: The report long, well written, and ignored it.
Although the report was long and well written, it was ignored.
Although the report was long and well written.
The report was long and was well written was ignored.
The report was long, it was well written, it was ignored.
questions.explanation: The best combination joins related ideas and uses a subordinate clause to show contrast, avoiding a comma splice or fragment.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: The exam; was long, nevertheless most of us finished.
The exam was long; because most of us finished.
The exam was long; nevertheless, most of us finished.
The exam was; long nevertheless, most of us finished.
The exam was long; and most of us finished.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two independent clauses; a conjunctive adverb such as "nevertheless" is followed by a comma.

questions.question: Which sentence is correct and most effective?
options: The staff, who had worked overtime for weeks deserved the bonus.
The staff who, had worked overtime for weeks deserved the bonus.
The staff, who worked overtime for weeks, they deserved the bonus.
The staff, who had worked overtime for weeks, deserved the bonus.
The staff who had worked overtime for weeks, deserved the bonus.
questions.explanation: The nonrestrictive clause needs commas at both ends, and no extra pronoun (they) should repeat the subject.

questions.question: Which sentence has an inconsistent shift in person?
options: If a person studies hard, he or she will pass the exam.
If you study hard, you will pass the exam.
If a student studies, the student will pass.
If people study hard, they will pass the exam.
If a person studies hard, you will pass the exam.
questions.explanation: The sentence shifts from third person (a person) to second person (you). Pronouns must stay consistent in person.

questions.question: Which is the best revision of this sentence? "The reason for the delay was because the truck broke down."
options: The delay occurred because the truck broke down.
The reason why the delay was because the truck broke down.
Because the truck broke down was the reason for the delay.
The reason for the delay was because the truck broke down.
The delay was a reason because the truck broke down.
questions.explanation: "The reason ... was because" is redundant and faulty; "because" already means "for the reason that," so a direct sentence is best.
